chapters.title: Thus Spoke Poet Kalidasa
paragraphs: The city where Byomkesh and I had come to spend a week in exile could well be called a coal-town. Encircling the city, at a distance of three or four miles, lay four or so coal mines. The city itself sat at the center, like a spider in its web, as coal from all directions was gathered at the railway station and dispatched by freight trains to distant places. It was a bustling, prosperous city; wealthy businessmen had set up their haunts here, several large banks operated, and lawyers, doctors, engineers, brokers, and moneylenders abounded. The streets bustled with motors, taxis, buses, and trucks. There was a constant exchange of raw materials and ready cash. The city was ruled—by coal. Everywhere, the song of coal, the clamor of coal. The city was by no means ancient, yet it seemed as if the invisible dust of coal had cast a premature shadow of age upon its every surface.

The man who had summoned us to this city was the owner of a coal mine called Phuljhari—his name, Manish Chakraborty. For several months, his mine had been plagued by various covert disturbances. Fires breaking out deep within the mine, valuable machinery being damaged and destroyed—such accidents had occurred; even among the laborers and coolies, needless discontent had begun to brew. There was no doubt that a group of people were trying to harm him. In such circumstances, as was only natural, Manish Babu called the police. He dismissed many new workers. But nothing came of it. At last, in secret, he sent for Byomkesh.

One evening in the month of Chaitra, we arrived at Manish Babu’s residence—a spacious, two-storied house surrounded by gardens, situated in the city’s most distinguished quarter. Manish Babu had just returned from the mine and greeted us cordially. He appeared to be around fifty, a fair-complexioned and handsome man, still in robust health. The firmness of his jaw suggested a somewhat stern temperament.

After we had sat conversing for a while in the drawing room, Manish Babu said, “Byomkesh Babu, you must stay here under assumed names. You will be Gagan Babu, and Ajit Babu will be Sujit Babu. If people hear your real names, they will immediately guess your purpose here. That would not be desirable.”
Byomkesh smiled and replied, “Very well, for as long as we are here, I shall be Gagan Babu. Ajit has no objection to becoming Sujit either.”
At the doorway, a young man stood shifting uneasily, perhaps waiting for an introduction to Byomkesh. Manish Babu called out, “Phani!”
The young man entered the room eagerly. Manish Babu turned to us and said, “My son, Phanish. —Phani, you know who they are, but make sure no one else outside the house finds out.”
Thus Spake Poet Kalidas 675
Phanish said, “No, sir.”
“Then take them to the guest room. See that they have no inconvenience. —You gentlemen, please wash your hands and faces, tea is being prepared.”

The guest room adjoined the drawing room. A large chamber, with two beds. Table, chairs, and other suitable furnishings arranged neatly, with an attached bathroom. Phanish led us to the room and lingered by the door.

The boy struck me as gentle and good-natured. Handsome like his father, but his body and mind had yet to reach full maturity; a trace of boyishness still clung to his mannerisms. He seemed to be about twenty-three or twenty-four.

As we changed our clothes, a few words were exchanged; Phanish answered Byomkesh’s questions shyly. He was his father’s only son, married just a year ago. Every day he accompanied his father to the coal mine to oversee the work. I noticed that, as he replied to Byomkesh, he seemed to be trying to say something else, but hesitated and fell silent out of embarrassment.
What Phanish wished to say remained unheard, for we returned to the sitting room. In the meantime, tea and refreshments had arrived; we took our seats.

At the tea table, however, there were no women to be seen—only the four of us. Yet there were certainly at least two women in the house. It seemed Manish Babu had not entirely renounced swadeshi customs. But in this modern, cosmopolitan age, is a little seclusion such a bad thing?

Having finished our refreshments and lit our cigarettes, a large car pulled up in front of the house. From it descended a middle-aged man. He had the appearance of a gorilla, with eyes ringed in darkness, slow and cunning. If it were possible to read character from a face, I would have said this man was a great villain.

Manish Babu welcomed the newcomer warmly, brought him into the room, and introduced us. “This is Mr. Gobinda Haldar, owner of one of the local coal mines. And these are Mr. Gagan Mitra and Sujit Bandyopadhyay; my friends, visiting from Calcutta.”
Gobinda Babu surveyed us with his Saturnine gaze, then said to Manish Babu, “I came to get the news. Any more trouble at the mine?”

Manish Babu replied gravely, “There’s always trouble. Night before last, another incident. Suddenly, the pump in Number Five Pit stopped working. Luckily, the watchmen were alert, so no great harm was done. Otherwise—”
Gobinda Babu clicked his tongue. Manish Babu said, “You seem to be doing well; all the mischief is reserved for my mine. I can’t understand why these wretches have their eyes fixed on me.”

Gobinda Babu replied, “There was trouble at my mine too, about six months ago. I knew the police would be useless, so I set spies directly. Planted eight men as informers, and within eight or nine days they brought me word of who was behind the mischief. Five ringleaders—had them brought in one day and gave them a good thrashing. Didn’t have to dismiss them; they ran off on their own. Since then, everything’s been quiet.” He gave a characteristic gorilla grin.

Manish Babu said, “I set spies too, but nothing came of it. Let’s leave that aside—” He changed the subject. Conversation drifted to more general matters. Tea and refreshments were brought for Gobinda Babu, which he partook of. Yet his eyes continued to roam about us.
Byomkesh Samagra
It seemed he did not quite believe that we had come here merely for a holiday.

After about an hour, he rose to leave. Manishbabu accompanied him to the car porch, and so did we. The driver opened the car door. Gobindababu, about to step into the car, turned his head towards Byomkesh with a half-smile and said, “Let’s see you try.” He got in, and the car drove away.
For a while, Manishbabu and we exchanged glances. Then, in a melancholy tone, he said, “Gobinda Haldar is a shrewd man. It’s not easy to pull the wool over his eyes.”
It was eleven by the time we finished dinner and retired for the night. The fatigue of the train journey still weighed on me. As soon as I lay down under the whirring fan, I sank into a deep sleep.
When I awoke the next morning, it was already eight o’clock.

A servant informed us that both the elder and the younger master had left for the colliery at dawn. We hurried through our morning ablutions and entered the outer room, where we found our tea and breakfast arranged on the table—and a young woman standing beside it.

We had not seen any of the women of the house before, so we were a little taken aback. In response to Byomkesh’s questioning glance, the girl lowered her head and said in a soft, hesitant voice, “I am Indira, the daughter-in-law of this house. Please, do eat.”

Phanish’s wife. Dusky-skinned, slender, her face fresh and youthful—she could not have been more than eighteen or nineteen. It was clear at a glance that Indira was a shy girl, unaccustomed to conversing freely with unfamiliar, older men. With no men left in the house, the poor girl had been compelled to come and attend to the guests.
We sat down to eat. Byomkesh said, “Why don’t you sit? Why are you standing?”
Indira perched on the edge of a sofa.
Byomkesh took a sip of tea to moisten his throat, then pulled the breakfast tray towards him. “We woke up late today. Does the master always leave so early?”
“Yes, Father leaves at seven,” she replied.
“And your husband?”
Indira’s head dropped at once. Without raising her eyes, she murmured, “He does too.”
Then, forcing herself to overcome her embarrassment, she added, “They return for lunch at twelve, then leave again at three.”

She glanced at Byomkesh with a faint, conspiratorial smile, but said nothing more. As I ate, I observed Indira. She sat quietly, occasionally casting a swift, sidelong glance at Byomkesh. It seemed to me she had some purpose beyond merely attending to guests. She knew who Byomkesh was—Phanish must have told her—and she wanted to say something to him. She had resolved something in her mind, but shyness held her back. I had noticed a similar hesitation on Phanish’s face last night.
After breakfast, Byomkesh took a final sip of tea, wiped his mouth with a handkerchief, and said in a gentle tone, “Well, what is it you want to say? Go on.”
I had been watching the struggle between resolve and embarrassment on Indira’s face. Now I saw her start in surprise, eyes wide, and, almost without realizing it, she stood up. Then all her...
A sigh of anxiety escaped in a single breath. “Byomkesh Babu, please save my husband. He is in grave danger.”
Byomkesh rose and sat down on the sofa, gesturing for Indira to sit beside him. “Sit. Tell me, what danger threatens your husband?”
Indira perched nervously on the edge of the sofa, her voice thin and restrained. “I—I can’t arrange all the words properly. If you help, he will tell you himself.”
Byomkesh asked, “Is it something to do with the mine?”
Indira replied, “No, something else. Please don’t tell my father anything. He knows nothing.”
Byomkesh assured her in a calm, soothing tone, “I won’t say a word to anyone. Don’t be afraid.”
“You will help him?”
“I don’t know anything yet. Still, if your husband is innocent, I will certainly help.”
“My husband is innocent.”
“Then have no fear.”
Along the side of the house, at the edge of the garden, stood a row of rooms. After a smile finally broke across Indira’s face, we made our way in that direction, drawing on our cigarettes.

From the front room emerged a middle-aged gentleman. He wore a Farashdanga dhoti and an addi panjabi, his appearance neat and trim. He must have used hair dye, for beneath the black hair, white roots were beginning to show.
Byomkesh said, “My name is Ganan Mitra, and this is Sujit Bandyopadhyay. Guests of Manish Babu.”
The gentleman greeted us with hurried hospitality. “Come in, come in. I heard from the master that you would be arriving. I am Surapati Ghatak, caretaker of this office.”
Surapatibabu did not know our real names. Byomkesh said, “This is the coal mine office, I presume. You are the office-master.”
Surapatibabu replied, “Yes, indeed. There is a small office at the coal mine itself, but this is the main office. Please, come and see.”

We inspected the rooms one by one. In various rooms, clerks worked over ledgers and papers, the clatter of typewriters filled the air—nothing particularly remarkable. After making the rounds, we finally sat down in Surapatibabu’s office.

After some general conversation, Byomkesh hesitated slightly before saying, “Let me tell you, my friend and I are thinking of buying a small coal mine together. Not here, in another district. We’re getting it cheap. But we have no idea how to run a coal mine; that’s why we’ve come to see Manish Babu’s mine. We want to gain some experience in office work, mining work, everything.”

Surapatibabu replied with great enthusiasm, “Of course, of course. That’s no trouble at all. You’ll learn the office work in two days; and mining work isn’t so difficult either. Besides, if you need, I can get you some very good men.”
Byomkesh asked, “What sort of men?”
Surapatibabu said, “Men who know office work, who know colliery work. People I’ve trained myself.”
Byomkesh showed interest. “Really! If we can get capable, experienced men—”
Byomkesh Samagra
We’ll discuss this with you. I’ll also look into the office work. We’ll be here for a few days now.’
I returned from the office.

At twelve, Phanish and Manish Babu came back from the mine. After their bath and meal, a bell rang somewhere in the house. Then, after a brief rest, the four of us boarded the motorcar and set off for the coal mine.
It was a large car. Phanish took the wheel, while the three of us sat in the back.
The motorcar left the city behind and took to a lonely road. The mine was about three miles away.
Byomkesh said, ‘I met Surapati Babu this morning. How long has he been working for you?’
Manish Babu replied, ‘Nearly twenty years. An experienced man.’
Byomkesh said, ‘I told him we’re looking to buy a coal mine. That we’re here to make inquiries. I didn’t reveal our true identity.’
Manish Babu said, ‘You did the right thing. Surapati is a trustworthy fellow, though, except for the fact that two years ago he took a second wife.’
So that explained Surapati Babu’s dyed hair and dandyish clothes. In middle age, it’s only natural to try and conjure the illusion of youth in the eyes of a young bride.
After a while spent in silence, Byomkesh asked, ‘Has anyone recently offered to buy your mine?’
Manish Babu replied, ‘Not recently, a few years back. A Marwari gentleman. He offered a good price, but I didn’t sell.’
Byomkesh asked a second question, ‘Do you have any dealings with the other mine owners around here?’
Manish Babu said, ‘I can’t claim to be on intimate terms, but I have no open quarrel with anyone.’
‘Is there anyone who, while wearing the mask of civility, secretly wishes you harm?’
‘There might be, but how would I know?’
‘True enough. The man who came last night—Govinda Haldar—what sort of person is he?’

Manish Babu replied in a slow, thoughtful voice, ‘Govinda Haldar is hard to read. Like a slippery fish, impossible to grasp. But Govinda Babu’s younger brother and partner, Aravinda, is a thoroughly bad lot. A drunkard, a gambler, a man of vile character. A few years ago his wife killed herself to escape his torment. Since then, Aravinda has become a notorious ruffian.’
No more was said. We entered the coal mine’s domain.

I have no desire to give a detailed description of the coal mine. Those who haven’t seen one with their own eyes have surely glimpsed it on stage or screen—it’s hardly a feast for the eyes. Especially since, in this tale, the mine’s role is minimal; it serves merely as the dark backdrop to our story. Without a backdrop, the narrative would stand naked, so it must remain.

Coal! The force that drives the machines is itself dragged from the deep womb of the earth by the power of machines; the wheels of civilization turn. Hail, machine. Your picks and shovels tear the earth’s flesh, scatter her entrails! Hail, machine. Enough.
We were introduced to the mine’s manager, Tarapada Babu. An elderly man, within the boundaries of the mine—
Kohen Kobikalidas 679

Residence; he strikes one as a grave, formidable man. He showed us the various workings of the mine. He even proposed that we descend into the bowels of the earth, but we declined. Sita had ample reason to enter the underworld; we have no such cause.

In the afternoon, we took tea in Tarapada Babu’s office. There we met the mine’s doctor, Jatindra Ghosh, and several other senior staff. No business was discussed; only general conversation drifted about. Needless to say, we remained under our assumed names. At one point, I noticed Byomkesh had struck up quite a rapport with Dr. Ghosh, sitting together in a corner, deep in conversation. Dr. Ghosh is of our own age, and he manages the dispensary and hospital attached to the mine. In his suit and trousers, there is a faint trace of weariness, as if life itself has left its mark.
When evening fell, we boarded the motorcar and set out once more for home.
After dinner that night, Manish Babu went upstairs to sleep, and we retired to our own room. Phanish came with us.
Byomkesh switched on the fan, stretched out on his bed, lit a cigarette, and said to Phanish, “Sit down. What’s going on? Why have you made your wife so anxious?”
Phanish sat in a chair, rubbing his hands nervously, then said in a hesitant voice, “I’d persuaded Indira to tell you herself—I didn’t have the courage—”
“But what is it? From the looks of things, it seems quite serious.”
“Yes, sir, it’s serious. By a twist of fate, I’ve become entangled in a murder case. If Father finds out—”
Byomkesh sat up on the bed. “A murder case?”
Phanish replied in a thin voice, “Yes, sir, it’s a nasty business. The police have started their investigation, and they’ve learned that we—”
“Tell us everything, from the beginning, in order.”
Of course, Phanish could not relate the whole story in an orderly fashion. His tale was tangled and confused; I shall do my best to set it down straight—

There is a club in this town. Out of jest, it has been named the ‘Coal Club’. The membership fee is steep, so only the well-to-do can belong. Phanish is a member. There are many other distinguished members; among them, Mrigendra Moulik, owner of the Uludanga coal mine, Madhumoy Sur of Dhoopipota mine, and Aravinda and Govinda Haldar of the Shimulia mine are especially notable.

In the afternoons, there is tennis and badminton at the club; after dusk, billiards, ping-pong, and cards and dice. Gambling on cards is common, but the club rules prohibit high stakes; so those with a gambler’s blood find little satisfaction. Aravinda Haldar is one of these restless souls. But what can be done? There is no other respectable den of gambling in town.

About a year ago, an elderly gentleman became a member of the club. A man of means, he had set up a moneylending business, a newcomer to the town. He kept a small office in the market district, but lived outside town, in a house by a lonely road. With a face like a vulture, his name was Pranahari Poddar.
Byomkesh Samagra

Poddar Mahashay would come and sit at the club. There were no other elderly gentlemen of his age there; most were young men, with a few of middle age. Gradually, he made the acquaintance of one or two. But, owing to the difference in age, he did not form any particular intimacy with anyone.

Phonish, Mrigen Moulik, Madhumoy Sur, and Aravinda Haldar—these four had formed a little group at the club. Phonish was the youngest among them, and Aravinda Haldar the eldest. He was about thirty-five; the leader of the group.

One evening, after dusk, they were sitting in a room at the club playing bridge, when Poddar Mahashay came and began to watch their game. Circling the table, he observed who had been dealt what kind of hand. Aravinda asked lazily, “Do you know contract bridge?”
The old man smiled a little and replied, “I do.”
“Will you play?”
“I will. What are the stakes?”
“One rupee a point. Is that all right?”
“That’s fine.”
When the current rubber ended, the players cut the cards and one of them stepped out. Pranahari Poddar took a seat at the table.

It soon became clear that Poddar Mahashay was a most skillful player. But that day, fortune did not favor him; he was not dealt good hands. At the end of the game, the accounts were tallied and it was found he had lost twenty-one rupees. He paid his debt at once.

From then on, Pranaharibabu would join Phonish’s group to play almost every day. Sometimes he lost, sometimes he won; in all circumstances, he remained unruffled. In this way, he became a member of Phonish’s circle.
Several months passed in this manner.
One day last Phalgun, as they sat down to play, Pranaharibabu said, “Don’t you play any other games besides bridge?”
Madhumoy Sur asked, “What sort of games?”
Pranahari replied, “For instance, poker or running flash.”
Mrigen Moulik said, “We know how to play them all. But gambling is not allowed at the club. Bridge isn’t gambling, after all, it’s a game of skill.” He gave a mocking laugh through his nose.
Pranahari said nothing then. When the game ended, he said, “Why don’t you come to my house one day? I’ll teach you a new game.”
No one objected. Aravinda said, “Why not? Where do you live?”
Pranahari replied, “My house is outside the city, on the Uludanga Khoni Road. I live alone—if you come, it’ll be lively. Why not come tomorrow?”
Everyone agreed. Pranahari hailed a taxi and left. He didn’t own a car; he had an arrangement with a taxi and always traveled by it.

The next evening, the four of them rode in Aravinda’s car and arrived at Pranahari’s house. The two-storied house stood on a deserted road, about a mile and a half beyond the city limits; there wasn’t another house within two or three hundred yards.
Pranaharibabu welcomed them with great hospitality, led them into a well-appointed room on the ground floor, and seated them. For a while, they conversed on general topics. Pranaharibabu
Kohen K Bi Kalidas
A widower, childless; he had previously lived in the city of Cuttack, Orissa. But his heart did not settle there, so he moved here. He has a maidservant with him, who cooks and tends to his needs.

At this moment, the maid entered, carrying a tray of tea. She set the tray down on the table and left, only to return with a plate of cutlets. A strikingly built young woman. Twenty or twenty-two years old; her complexion dusky, but her face beautiful, her eyes filled with the enchantment of a doe. At first glance, one would not take her for a mere servant girl. As she passed among the guests, she left a ripple of restlessness in her wake.
Sipping tea with the hot cutlets, Aravind remarked, “Splendid cutlets she’s fried. Is she your maid?”
Pranharibabu replied, “Yes. I brought Mohini from Orissa. She cooks well.”

After refreshments, the game began. By unanimous agreement, a three-card game of running flush commenced. Everyone had brought extra money; Pranharibabu sat down with five hundred rupees in hand. The game lasted two hours. There were no great wins or losses; one won fifty rupees, another lost a hundred. Pranharibabu, on the whole, ended up losing. It was decided that in three days, the game would be held here again.

But Phanish was not happy. He liked playing cards, true, but he was no gambler. He had a strict father hovering over him; he was not entirely free with money matters. He had been drawn into this gambling circle by the force of the group, but if he tried to leave, he would become a laughingstock. Phanish remained reluctantly bound to the gambling party.

On the second day, the game was livelier than ever. Mohini had prepared chicken fry. The game began as they ate it with tea; midway through, Pranharibabu produced a bottle of imported whisky. Phanish could not tolerate liquor—if he drank, he would vomit—so he abstained. The others drank. Aravind drank the most. The stakes of the game climbed higher and higher. Everyone grew excited, except for Pranharibabu, who remained impassive.
At the end of the game, the tally was made: Aravind had won nearly a thousand rupees, while everyone else had lost. Pranharibabu had won two hundred rupees.
Thereafter, the game was held once or twice a week. Some days one would lose, some days another, the rest would win. Pranharibabu never lost much; overall, he always profited.

Alongside the gambling, another drama had begun to unfold—this one involving Mohini. Madhumoy and Mrigendra may have been secretly drawn to Mohini, but Aravind pursued her openly and shamelessly. On game days, he would arrive at Pranharibabu’s house before anyone else and stand by the kitchen door, flirting with Mohini. It was even suspected that, during the day, in Pranharibabu’s absence, he would visit the house. How intimate Aravind and Mohini had become was impossible to say, but given Mohini’s station, it was unlikely she would spurn the attentions of a man of means.

Thus, five or six weeks passed. Phanish found no peace; he tried to avoid his friends, but could not—Aravind would drag him along. Then, one day, everyone’s eyes were opened. They discovered that Pranharibabu was a seasoned card-sharp, a master of sleight of hand. There was quite a quarrel, and then the guests abandoned the game and left.
Byomkesh Samagra

It was learned that each of the guests had lost three to four thousand rupees, and all the money had vanished into Pranahari’s coffers. Aravind had lost the most—almost five thousand rupees. Sitting in the club, Aravind fumed, “Let that old vulture show his face—I’ll break his bones to powder.” Madhumoy and Mrigen said nothing, but their expressions made it clear that if they got their hands on Pranahari, they wouldn’t let him off easily either.
But Pranahari Babu was a shrewd man; he never set foot in the club again.
About a week later, Aravind said, “The scoundrel’s gone into hiding. Let’s go to his house and teach him a lesson.”
Phanish objected, “What’s the point? The money’s gone—what’s done is done.”
Aravind replied, “Money is dirt on our hands. But are we to let the bastard cheat us and walk away? What do you say, Mrigen?”
Mrigen said, “He needs to be taught a lesson.”
Madhumoy added, “There’s no one in his house except a woman. Nothing to be afraid of.”

Around eight in the evening, the four of them set out. From the taxi stand not far from the club, they hired a taxi and headed toward Pranahari’s house. It wasn’t wise to take their own car; though the road was lonely, at night many vehicles traveled from the Uludanga Colliery. If anyone saw a familiar car near Pranahari’s house, it would raise suspicion. Besides, chauffeurs aren’t deaf-mutes—they’d gossip. If you’re going to rough someone up, it’s best to have as few witnesses as possible.

They stopped the taxi a hundred yards from Pranahari’s house and got out. The road was deserted. Madhumoy carried a large electric torch, which he flicked on and off as they advanced toward the house, telling the taxi driver to turn the car around and wait.

There was light in the upstairs room. The main door below was open. From the kitchen came the hiss and sputter of cooking—Mohini was preparing dinner. The four slipped in like hunters, silent and alert.

The entrance hall was long, with a staircase on the left leading to the second floor. Here, they paused and conferred in low voices. Then Aravind took the torch from Madhumoy and crept upstairs, treading softly. After a while, he returned and said, “There’s a door at the top of the stairs—a sturdy one. Can’t tell if it’s locked from inside or out. There’s a Yale lock on it.”
After more discussion, they decided to search the ground floor thoroughly. The old man was cunning; perhaps he’d left the light burning upstairs and was hiding somewhere in the darkness below.
Aravind peeked into the kitchen—Mohini stood alone, her back to the door, cooking. No one else was there.
Then, the four began to search the rooms and the open yard at the back, each going their separate ways.
Fifteen minutes later, they all gathered again at the foot of the stairs. No one had found Pranahari. So, the old man must be upstairs. Aravind said, “Come on, let’s try the door again.”
This time, all four climbed the stairs. As soon as they pressed on the door, it swung open.
Light filled the room. In the middle of the floor, Pranahari Poddar lay sprawled on his side. On the right side of his sparse-haired head was a long, bloody gash, as if he had—
Kohen K Bi Kalidas 683
A parting down the right side of her hair, vermilion smeared along the line. Her face contorted, teeth missing; Pranahari, lying on his deathbed, was making faces at the onlookers.
For a moment, the four of them stood frozen, then, all at once, they tumbled down the stairs in a rush. Out onto the street.

Approaching the taxi, they saw the driver slumped over the steering wheel, fast asleep. Each pressed a finger to his lips, warning the others to silence, then quietly climbed into the car. The driver woke and started the engine.

When the four returned to the club, it was only nine o’clock. They sat together in a secluded corner and conferred: there was no need to tell anyone anything. News of Pranahari’s accidental death would, of course, become public, but there was no evidence that the four of them had visited his house. The taxi driver had waited a hundred yards away. He hadn’t seen them enter Pranahari’s home. Therefore, it was wise to keep the adventure buried in their consciences.

That night, they played cards at the club until half past ten, then returned home, as if nothing had happened. The next day, news of Pranahari’s death spread through the city, but the names of these four were not linked to the murder. On the third day, the police raided Aravinda’s house. How the police had found out, none could say.

But all four were men of great influence in the city; so far, none had been caught. The matter had not become public knowledge. The police were conducting a vigorous investigation, questioning each of them in turn. Anything could happen at any time. Phanish’s situation was dire. On one hand, the charge of murder; on the other, if his strict father were to learn that he gambled and was entangled in a murder case—who could say what he might do, and so on, and so forth.

By the time Phanish finished his tale, it was midnight. Reassuring him, Byomkesh said, “Tell your wife there’s nothing to worry about. I take responsibility for uncovering the truth. Tomorrow we’ll go into the city; we’ll need a car.”
Phanish replied, “I’ll tell the driver—the small car will be at your disposal.”
Phanish departed. We turned off the lights and went to bed. Lying on his own cot, Byomkesh lit a cigarette and drew on it softly.
I asked, “What do you make of it?”
Byomkesh said, “Of the five suspects, I’ve seen only one. Until I see the other four, it’s hard to say anything.”
“Five suspects!”
“Yes. We can’t rule out the maidservant.”
Nothing more was said. Thinking of the strange conclusion to Pranahari Poddar’s life, I drifted off to sleep.

In the morning, I awoke to find Byomkesh seated at the table, writing a letter with utmost concentration. Stretching and yawning, I asked, “Who are you writing to? Satyabati? Barely two days apart and already you’re pining for her?”
Byomkesh, still writing, replied, “Not longing—Bikash.”
“Bikash?”
“Yes—Bikash. Why are you writing to him?”
Byomkesh Samagra

“I’ve arranged a job for Bikash. A compounder’s position at the colliery’s dispensary. That’s why I’m writing to ask him to come.” “I see.” Byomkesh returned to his letter. He wanted to bring Bikash here and install him at the colliery, while he himself would remain at a distance, gathering intelligence about the mine. The answer came, “I’ve discovered three facts. One—the person who killed Pranahari Poddar was not motivated by money; two—he is ambidextrous; three—for a woman like Mohini, anyone could commit murder. Now go to sleep.”
In the morning, I woke to find Byomkesh already seated with the account book. After breakfast, we set out as usual. Byomkesh took the account book along.
At the thana, Inspector Barat greeted us with a smile. “Finished with the account book already?”

Byomkesh said, “Nothing that sheds light on the murder. But there’s a small detail that bothers me.”

On each page, side by side, were columns for credits and expenses. In the expenses column, entries went down to a single paisa or two, but most days the credit column was empty. Bhuban said, “I don’t know much, sir. He had an office in the city. About a year ago, he called me and proposed hiring the taxi on a monthly basis—I agreed. “You agreed to a monthly wage of only thirty-five rupees? Was there any profit in it?”

Phanish replied, “That one playing there, in the blue vest and white trousers, that’s Mrigen—”

As we sipped the ice-cold sharbat, I felt a pleasant dizziness creeping in. Outside, the tennis match ended. The club members began coming in, snatches of conversation drifting to our ears. Inside the house, electric lights blazed in every room. From the table-tennis room came the sharp clack of play. Suddenly, a member’s voice rang out—Hey, bearer!
A living tableau of affluent, genteel life.

When the sharbat was finished, we lit cigarettes and entered the house. In the central hall, two silent players were absorbed in a languid game of billiards; on the vast table, three balls played hide-and-seek like children. —Here, there was no one of interest to us.

Phanish whispered, “The one who bid is Madhumoy Sur, and his partner is Aravind Halder.”

The same gorilla-like features, only younger. Madhumoy Sur was a dapper, fastidious man; the lack of character in his face was compensated for by his immaculate, tailored panjabi and diamond buttons.
The game had begun, one of the opposing team had become dummy. It was a slam, and no one’s attention strayed elsewhere.

After watching for five minutes, Byomkesh signaled, and we stepped outside. He did not seem satisfied with the possible suspects he had observed; in a dry tone, he said, “We’ve seen what there was to see. Let’s go home now.”
On our way back in the car, I asked, “What did you see?”

Byomkesh replied, “I saw three men, their surroundings, the way they moved their hands and feet. —Phanish, tomorrow morning we’ll visit their homes. It’s necessary to make their acquaintance. I don’t expect to get more than what we have today, but still—”
“So you did get something today?”
“I did. Though it’s negative evidence.”
The next morning, Phanish did not go to the coal mine with his father; Manish Babu went alone. Phanish drove us himself. Starting the car, he asked, “Where shall we go first?”
Byomkesh said, “I have no preference for any of them. Let’s visit the one whose house is nearest.”
“In that case, let’s go to Mrigen Babu’s house.”

Mrigen Moulik’s house was exceedingly elegant, a testament to the owner’s refined taste. Our car passed through the garden and stopped at the portico. We saw Mrigen Moulik reclining in an easy chair in front of the house, reading the newspaper, dressed in loose pajamas and a silk dressing gown. As we got out of the car, he folded the paper and looked up at us. No smile of welcome appeared on his face; rather, his expression darkened. When we approached, he said in a harsh voice, “What do you want?”
We halted, startled. Phanish said, “Mrigenbabu, these are my father’s friends, come from Calcutta—”
Casting a look of fierce contempt at Phanish, Mrigen said, “I know. Which one is Byomkesh Bakshi?”
Phanish faltered. Byomkesh replied, “I am Byomkesh Bakshi. I had a few words for you.”
Mrigen twisted his face in utter disdain and said, “Nothing will be accomplished here. You may leave.” With that, he tucked the paper under his arm and strode into the house.
We looked at each other. Phanish’s face had turned the color of vermilion from humiliation, while a wounded smile played on Byomkesh’s lips. He said, “I see Govinda Haldar has warned the suspects.”
Phanish said, “Let’s go home.”

Byomkesh shook his head. “No, since we’re out, we’ll finish our work before returning. Don’t be ashamed, Phanish. Those who seek the truth must abandon shame, hatred, and fear. Come, let’s go to Madhumoy Sur’s house next.”
As we made our way to the car, I said, “But why? What does this behavior mean? If Mrigen Maulik is innocent, what is he afraid of?”
Byomkesh said, “They think I’m on Phanish’s side, that I want to save him and implicate them.”

Madhumoy Sur’s house had the air of late afternoon, the garden devoid of any charm. On the front veranda, Madhumoy Sur lay on a mat, clad in a gamchha, while a burly young servant massaged his body with oil. Phanish began, his voice thin and hesitant, “Madhumoybabu, forgive us, this is your bathing hour—”

With that, Madhumoy Sur prepared to recline again.
Byomkesh said, “But the taxi driver identified you.”
Madhumoy replied, “The taxi driver is a liar. —Now, please, namaskar.”
Byomkesh quickly asked, “Do you own a torch?”
Madhumoy said, “I have five torches. Now, please, namaskar.”

As we headed toward Aravinda Haldar’s house, Byomkesh remarked, “Madhumoy knew we would come, had rehearsed what to say. Whatever else, he’s more civil than Mrigen Maulik. How sweetly he said—‘Now, please, namaskar.’ In the words of Nimchand Dutta—‘The boy is not ill-mannered.’”

Outwardly, Bhuvan appeared calm and collected, but within him simmered a fierce, concealed pride. He would never tolerate an insult to his wife. Mohini, that girl, was remarkably astute. Even at the sight of a corpse, she did not lose her head; she instantly determined her course of action. Whoever the murderer was, the police must not catch him. Mohini was certain the killer had entered and exited through the bathroom door. She had no doubt about it. She locked the two back doors from the inside, then sent word to the police through the truck driver. What a formidable woman—she did not overdo a single thing. She did exactly as much as was needed to mislead the police.

Mohini lied to us many times, but never unnecessarily. Bhuvan was the same. I am convinced that on the very night of the murder, at some point, Bhuvan returned and told Mohini everything, and from then on, he visited her frequently. That is why Mohini did not want to leave the house after the murder. It was absolutely necessary for her to maintain contact with Bhuvan.

At any rate, when I entered the stage, the police’s suspicious gaze had already settled on the four accused. Motive and opportunity—both were present in abundance. Either these four had conspired together to commit the murder, or one of them had done it, throwing dust in the eyes of the others. I had no reason to disagree with the police; yet, the idea of a collective murder was hard to digest. The suspects were not dacoits from central India—they were so-called civilized members of society. They would not band together to kill.

But one among them could have murdered, deceiving the other three. The question was: who? The greatest suspicion fell upon Aravind Halder. He had not only lost at gambling, but had been cheated in another matter as well—one so shameful that he could never admit it to anyone. The shame of a libertine is a strange thing; he feels it only when, after spending two thousand rupees, he fails to obtain the object of his shameless desire.

As I began my investigation, a particular question troubled me. The first thing that came to mind was—where had the murder weapon gone? Dr. Ghoshal had described the weapon in detail, but no such object was found. If someone from Aravind’s group had brought the weapon, Phanish and Bhuvan could not have failed to notice. Therefore, they had not brought it, nor had they taken it away. Then where did it come from, and where did it go?

Secondly, from Dr. Ghoshal’s statement, it was clear to me that the murderer was left-handed. Think about it—there wasn’t even a chair in Pranahari’s bedroom; it was not believable that he would be sitting at the edge of the bed with his back turned to the assailant. The attacker had struck him face-to-face, the blow landing on the right side of his head, along the parting of his hair. Therefore, the assailant was left-handed, his left hand dominant.

I set out to find which of the four accused was left-handed. At the Coal Club, I saw Mrigen Maulik playing tennis with his right hand, Madhumoy Sur and Aravind Halder dealing and playing cards with their right hands. Then, when I tossed a glass paperweight to Phanish, he caught it with his right hand as well. None of them were left-handed.

But even if not left-handed, one of them could be ambidextrous. So I could not rule them out entirely. There were no other suspects. Mohini had not committed the murder; if she had wanted to kill Pranahari, she would have poisoned him. She had no motive.
I was at a loss, unable to find a direction—when, in a single moment, everything became clear.
As if a bolt of lightning had flashed across a cloud-shrouded, pitch-dark night. I saw Bhuban crouched by his taxi, a jack wedged beneath the wheel, turning it with his left hand!

We all knew that on the night of the murder, Bhubaneshwar Das, the taxi driver, had been present at the scene. Yet, not once had he crossed our minds. This is what G. K. Chesterton called the Invisible Man.
The problem of the weapon was solved in an instant. Bhuban had killed Pranahari with a spanner; the murder weapon matched Dr. Ghoshal’s description exactly.

Bhuban has fled with his wife. A shrewd man—he realized I had seen through him. Where they will set up their hideout, I cannot say; there are so many places—Madras, Bombay. I hope Pramodbabu never finds Bhuban. For if he does, he certainly won’t be awarding him a gold medal.

There is nothing more to say. If I have left anything out, you can guess at it yourselves. Bhuban and Mohini will remain fugitives for life, unless they are caught. The cruel greed of Pranahari Poddar has destroyed two lives—that is the greatest tragedy in this tale.
